faqs: Four kinds of buyers, in our grouping: AI labs such as OpenAI, which partnered with Reddit and News Corp, and Meta, which licenses datasets from third parties; data libraries such as Shutterstock, which license stock media; marketplaces such as Human Native and AWS Data Exchange; and brokers that collect internal company files, as Wired reported on November 6, 2026.
How much do AI companies pay for data?

Few prices are public. The clearest is Reddit's 2024 Form S-1: data licensing contracts with an aggregate value of $203.0 million, signed in January 2024 for two to three years, with at least $66.4 million expected as 2024 revenue. The filing does not name the buyers, so it is not a price list for AI labs, and it describes a huge platform, not a typical company.
Can a small or mid size company sell data to AI companies?

In our view, sometimes, mainly through marketplaces or brokers rather than direct lab deals. Internal records such as support tickets, SOPs and process histories are the kind labs cannot crawl, but they need a rights check and anonymization before anything is shared.
What is an AI data marketplace?

A platform that lists data from many owners so AI developers can find and pay for it. Cloudflare bought Human Native, which it called "an AI data marketplace that connects creators and AI developers", in January 2026. AWS Data Exchange is a general data marketplace whose buyers can use data for machine learning.

OpenAI licenses content from partners. Its May 2024 announcements say it will access Reddit's Data API and receive current and archived content from News Corp titles such as The Wall Street Journal. Neither announcement states a price, and the Reddit one does not mention training.
Is it safe to sell company files to a data broker?

It depends on the contract and on what you share. Check who the end buyer is, whether use is limited to training, whether personal data is removed first, and whether your customer contracts allow it. We found no published broker price lists, so get every term in writing. This is general information, not legal advice.
body:
Short answer. Four kinds of buyers pay for AI training data: AI labs that license directly from platforms and publishers, data libraries that license stock media, marketplaces that match data owners with AI developers, and brokers who collect internal company files to help train AI models (our grouping). The largest figure in the sources we read is a seller's: in its Form S-1 Reddit disclosed data licensing contracts worth $203.0 million, signed in January 2024 for terms of two to three years, without naming the buyers. Meta says plainly that "some datasets are purchased or licensed from third parties".

For an established company, the useful question is not who the biggest buyer is but which route can reach your records. A platform with millions of users can call a lab. In our view, a 100 person firm with ten years of support tickets usually cannot. Our AI data licensing service exists for that second case.

This guide explains each kind of buyer from its own pages and filings, what each one pays for, and which route fits a mid size company. We do not rank brokers or marketplaces: in the pages we read, none published prices per record or sales volumes, which a fair ranking would need. Sources were read on November 24, 2026. This is general information, not legal advice.

The four kinds of AI training data buyers

Each kind of buyer wants something slightly different and reaches sellers in a different way. The table sums up what the primary sources below show.

BuyerWhat it buysHow sellers reach itExample from a primary source
AI labs, directlyPlatform and publisher content, plus commercial datasetsOne to one partnerships, so far with big platforms and publishersOpenAI's partnerships with Reddit and News Corp (May 2024); Meta's licensed datasets
Data librariesLicensed images, video, audio and moreA research or a commercial data license from the libraryShutterstock names OpenAI, Runway and ElevenLabs as users
MarketplacesData from many owners, listed or priced in one placeRegister as a provider and list or price your dataHuman Native (bought by Cloudflare, January 2026); AWS Data Exchange
BrokersInternal corporate files, such as work files and emailsNot published; agree terms one to oneWired, November 6, 2026: brokers collecting corporate files

In our view the lines blur: a library sells to labs, and a marketplace can act like a broker when it prepares the data itself. What matters for you is who signs the license with you and who ends up using the data.

AI labs that license data directly

The labs themselves are the end buyers. Meta's transparency page says its AI uses "a mix of publicly available data, licensed data and information from Meta's products and services", and that some datasets "are purchased or licensed from third parties, including commercial datasets and partner content".

OpenAI's own announcements show what direct deals look like. On May 16, 2024 it said it "will access Reddit's Data API, which provides real-time, structured, and unique content from Reddit", and that it would also become a Reddit advertising partner. On May 22, 2024 it announced a multi year agreement under which it "will receive access to current and archived content" from News Corp titles including The Wall Street Journal, Barron's, the New York Post and The Times. The Reddit post does not mention training. Neither announcement gives a price, and the Reddit post discloses that Sam Altman is a Reddit shareholder.

The one deal value in the filings we read comes from the seller's side. Reddit's Form S-1 says: "In January 2024, we entered into certain data licensing arrangements with an aggregate contract value of $203.0 million and terms ranging from two to three years." It expected at least $66.4 million of that as revenue in 2024, about 32.7% of the total by our arithmetic. Spread evenly, $203.0 million over two to three years works out to roughly $68 million to $102 million a year. The filing says only that third parties may "access, search, and analyze data" on the platform; it does not name the buyers, so we cannot say how much of the money came from AI labs.

Our reading of these pages: the direct deals made public so far are with sources that have scale, fresh content and a brand. A typical company is not in that position, which is why the next three routes exist. For the clauses a direct license should carry, see our guide to the AI data licensing agreement.

Data libraries that license stock media

Stock libraries now sell training data too. Shutterstock's release of March 19, 2026 says its data powers "systems built by some of the world's largest technology companies, including OpenAI", and that it supports companies such as Black Forest Labs, Runway and ElevenLabs. Its catalog, per the same release, covers images, video, audio, 3D content, templates, fonts, long form video, metadata, podcasts and science imagery.

The release also shows how Shutterstock structures licenses. Shutterstock "offers both research and commercial data licensing options", with researchers and startups starting on a research license before moving to a commercial license "for scaled deployment". Shutterstock sells this data, so in our view it has a stake in describing demand as strong.

We think that for a company outside media, a library matters mainly as a model of what buyers expect: clear rights, labels and a record of where each item came from.

Marketplaces that match data owners with AI developers

Marketplaces aim at a problem Cloudflare described when it launched pay per crawl on July 1, 2025. Publishers, it wrote, want AI crawlers to pay for access, and "currently, that requires knowing the right individual and striking a one-off deal, which is an insurmountable challenge if you don't have scale and leverage".

  • Human Native. On January 15, 2026 Cloudflare announced it had acquired Human Native, "an AI data marketplace that connects creators and AI developers", founded in 2024. Cloudflare said the deal would help publishers surface their data "to AI companies willing to pay". No price for the acquisition was given.
  • Pay per crawl. In the version Cloudflare described in July 2025 as a private beta, a site owner can set "a flat, per-request price across their entire site" and choose to allow, charge or block each crawler. A crawler that sends payment intent gets the page (HTTP 200); one that does not receives an HTTP 402 Payment Required response with the price. Cloudflare acts as the merchant of record. This sells access to public web pages, not internal records.
  • AWS Data Exchange. A general data marketplace rather than an AI one. Amazon's documentation says buyers can use data sets with "machine learning", and that to sell data in AWS Marketplace a provider must register and meet the legal eligibility requirements in the AWS Marketplace seller terms. Its publishing guidelines bar any data that can trace a device or an identifiable person to a sensitive location such as a cancer treatment center, a place of worship or a military base.

In our view a marketplace lowers the cost of finding a buyer, but it does not do your rights check for you. AWS says it "removes any product that breaches these guidelines".

Brokers who collect company files

Another kind of buyer wants what was never on the web. On November 6, 2026 Wired ran a story by Steven Levy under the headline "AI Companies Really, Really Want to Buy Your Work Files and Emails", reporting that data brokers are collecting all sorts of internal corporate files to help train AI models, and that not everyone is happy about it. The full story is for subscribers, so we use only its headline and summary here.

In our view this is the route most likely to reach a mid size company directly. It is also the one with the least public information: we found no published broker price list, and work files and emails are often full of personal data and confidential terms. Before you answer a broker, we would check four things:

  1. Who the end buyer is, and whether the contract limits use to training.
  2. What leaves your systems, and whether personal data is removed or anonymized first.
  3. Whether your customer contracts and privacy notice allow it. Our guide to the data sharing agreement versus a data license covers the difference.
  4. How you are paid: a one time fee, a share of the broker's revenue, or both, and when.

Which route fits a mid size company

Our view, based on the sources above: the route depends on what you hold and how much of it.

What you holdRoute that usually fitsWhy
A large public platform or archiveDirect deal with a labOpenAI's announced partnerships were with Reddit and News Corp, both large
Public web pagesCrawler controls or pay per crawlYou sell access to pages, not files
Licensed media (images, audio, video)A data library or marketplaceThey already handle rights and labels
Internal records (tickets, SOPs, CRM history)A broker or a prepared direct offerLabs cannot crawl this data; it needs anonymizing first

If your records sit in the last row, start with an inventory and a rights check before you talk to any buyer. Our step by step guide on how to sell data to AI companies covers the sequence, and where AI training data comes from explains why labs now pay for data they cannot crawl. If you would rather keep crawlers away from your public site, see our guide to blocking AI bots with Cloudflare.

What we could not verify

  • Prices per record, per document or per token: none appeared in the lab, library or marketplace pages we read.
  • Who bought Reddit's data: the S-1 does not name the buyers, and we could not verify reports of specific buyers.
  • Whether Cloudflare pay per crawl is still in private beta today: we describe it as announced in July 2025.
  • The body of the Wired story, which is for subscribers only.
